examples.english: Either because he who lent the book forgot it, or because it shames one to give it back stained or torn, or even because, as it happens a lot, he is a bibliophile for whom it is difficult to separate himself from a book that spent time in his hand, the fact is that for one or another of these reasons and many more, books lent to others rarely return to their place: in the library of who borrowed them.

examples.text: […] I el kijo azer lo mizmo, komo un buen kavayero, adjustar al suyo el nombre de la suya, i yamarse “don Kishot de la Mancha”, ke asegun el, deklarava klaramente su linaje i patria, i la onorava en tomandola por alkunya.

examples.text: Este es un kuento atado a una eksperiensa emosional sovrenatural, ke sea una eksperiensa emosional sovrenatural, ke sea una eksperiensa emosional relijioza personal, komo por exemplo un kuento sovre un santo sovrenatural o sovre un amahamiento mirakolozo, ke se trate de una eksperiensia emosional de un enkontro kon un ser sovrenatural o de un ser de otro mundo, komo un guerko o un fantazma.
examples.ref: 2006, Matilda Koén-Sarano, Por el plazer de kontar, Nur Afakot, page 28:
examples.english: This is an account connected to an emotional supernatural experience, whether it be an emotional supernatural experience, or a personal emotional religious experience, as for example an account about a supernatural saint or about a miracle cure, it is about an emotional experience from an encounter with a supernatural being or a being from another world, like a demon or a ghost.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish nada (“nothing”), inherited from Latin (nūlla rēs) nāta (literally “no born thing, not a thing born”), an extension of nēmō nātus (“not a soul”, literally “nobody born”). For descendants of the other part of the expression see Galician ren (“nothing”), French rien (“nothing”), Catalan res (“nothing; anything”). For the grammaticalization of an original nominal as a negative see Jespersen's Cycle and French personne, pas.

examples.text: En esta ensiklopedia es kontado, entre otras, ke en segito a los pogromes echos en Polonia, en los anyos 1648-1649, los djudios de Turkia embezaron⁷ sovre la triste suerte de miles de djudios ke avian kayido en kativerio i ke estavan en peligro de ser vendidos komo esklavos.

examples.translation: It says in this encyclopedia that, among other things, following the pogroms committed in Poland from 1648-1649, Turkey's Jews learned of the misfortune of thousands of Jews who fell into captivity and were in danger of being sold as slaves.

examples.translation: They were two brothers in Balat. The [first] one became a dentist, the other became a GP; after that he had become a pediatrician.

examples.text: I el sol es de dos modos kontrarios uno de otro, ke la parte ke esta para la tierra es de fuego, ma la otra parte ke da para el sielo es de pedrisko, ke kon esto se konserva uno kon otro, i el envierno tiene la vanda del pedrisko para la tierra i ansi aze muncho friyo, i si no fuera ke la otra vanda es de fuego, no era posivle ke pudieran la djente sonportarlo.
examples.ref: 2013 November 30, Jacobo Sefamí, Miriam Moscona, Por mi boka: Textos de la diáspora sefardí en ladino, Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial México, →ISBN, page 66:
examples.english: And the sun is of two phases contrary to one another: the part for the earth is fire, yet the other part for the sky is hail, one with the other is kept with this, and winter has hail’s side for the earth, making it very cold, and if it weren’t for the other side, the fiery one, it would not be possible that people could bear it.

etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish nadi, nade (“no one”), inherited from Latin nātī (“born men/people”), perfect past participle of nāscor (“to be born”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.
The semantic change is due to commonly being used with negated verbs in spoken Ibero-Romance, supposing for example *nātī nōn fēcērunt (“born [people] did not do it”), cognate with Old Galician-Portuguese nado (“no one”). Compare the development of French personne from “person” to “no one”. Old Spanish commonly also used the phrase omne nado. Nada (“nothing”) also originates from the same root, from (rēs) nāta (“born thing”); see Jespersen's Cycle. The final unstressed vowel was influenced by quién/quien (see Spanish) and alguién (today alguien) (see Spanish) towards the very end of the Old Spanish period: the earliest attestation of the -ie form is from c. 1253 in a Spanish translation of Syntipas known as Sendebar.

etymology_text:
Unknown. Cognate to Portuguese lesto (“agile”), Catalan llest (“clever; ready”), Italian lesto (“quick”), Maltese lest (“ready”).
* If "clever" be the original sense, probably from Proto-Germanic *listiz; compare Old High German and Old English list, both "knowledge, experience, cunning, art, trick, slyness" (see English list). A semantic development "clever" → "quick" → "ready" is very plausible, but note that the association with "cleverness" apparently exists only in Catalan, Ladino and Spanish (and might thus be secondary). Note also Irish cliste (“clever”).
* Alternatively, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *lextus or *lestus, reduced from *lexitus, as an alteration of Latin lēctus (“chosen; read”), participle of legō.

glosses: ready; set; all set; prepared; poised; up; down (with estar)

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish ladino, variant of latino. In mediaeval Spain, both ladino and latino could refer to either Spanish or Latin, since most early Romance speakers thought that their languages were simply Latin. A similar tendency persisted in Judezmo (see for example the Ferrara Bible); many Sephardim thought that their language was simply Castilian or Spanish.

examples.text: I presto se aleḇantaron kon una kandela a kada uno en sus mano i se fueron a buxkar en todas las kamaretas, de lugar en lugar puede ser toparán alguna koza de ḥamman i no toparon ninguna koza, i nunka les pasó por idea ke en akea kaxa ke le dyo el rey ke aḇía koza de ḥamman adientro de elya, por razón ke elyos ya saḇían ke estaḇa yena de ŷolyas i de piedras ḇalutozas.
examples.ref: 1991, Miscelánea de estudios árabes y hebraicos, volumes 37–38, Universidad de Granada, →ISBN, page 20:
examples.english: And they quickly rose with a candle in each of their hands and left to search every room, from place to place they shall maybe find something from Haman; they found nothing, and it never occurred to them that in that box that the king gave him there was something from Haman inside of it, because they already knew that it was full of jewels and precious stones.
examples.translation: And they quickly rose with a candle in each of their hands and left to search every room, from place to place they shall maybe find something from Haman; they found nothing, and it never occurred to them that in that box that the king gave him there was something from Haman inside of it, because they already knew that it was full of jewels and precious stones.

examples.text: Y esta fue la razón que en caśa, bueno, yo continuaba a hablar con mi padre y mi madre; y mis hijos sintían ladino en caśa y saben algunas palabras; entienden, ma no hablan, porque ellos continuaron solamente con el heḅreo. La razón es reunir una lingua para un pueblo, para un estado.
examples.ref: 2008, Margalit Matitiahu, edited by Iacob M. Hassán, Ricardo Izquierdo Benito, Elena Romero, Sefardíes: Literatura y lengua de una nación dispersa, Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha, →ISBN, page 153:
examples.english: And this was the reason that in [my] house, well, I kept speaking with my parents, and my children heard Judezmo at home and they know some words; they understand, yet do not speak [it], since they only stuck with Hebrew. The reason is to reunite a language for a people, for a state.
examples.translation: And this was the reason that in [my] house, well, I kept speaking with my parents, and my children heard Judezmo at home and they know some words; they understand, yet do not speak [it], since they only stuck with Hebrew. The reason is to reunite a language for a people, for a state.

examples.text: I ala onze [6 AM], ala turka, vinyeron en grande akompanyamyento delos askyeres turkos adelantre i detras, kompanyas de soldados de kada nasyon ke fueron dezbarkados delas naves, djunto todos los viche-amirales i komandantes, i ofisyeres de kada nave ke se topo en muestro porto.

head_templates.expansion: enemigo m (Hebrew spelling אינימיגו, feminine enemiga)

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish enemigo (“fiend”), from Latin inimīcus, from in- & amīcus (“friend”).

examples.text:
Sus enemigos, sus bienes, le rovaron.
De su bien si artaron i la espujaron ¹)
I con croeldades su corason razgaron
I eia no abandona sus tradisiones.
Termine la aniada i sus maldisiones.
examples.ref: 1910, Reuben Eliyahu Israel, Traducsion libera de las poezias ebraicas de Roş Aşana i Kipur, Craiova: Institutul Grafic, I. Samitca şi D. Baraş, Socieatate in Comandita, →OCLC, page 9:
examples.english: Her foes stole her properties. They were satiated with her property, [then] they engaged her, and they cruelly ripped her heart, [yet] she abandoned not her traditions. End the year and its curses.
examples.translation: Her foes stole her properties. They were satiated with her property, [then] they engaged her, and they cruelly ripped her heart, [yet] she abandoned not her traditions. End the year and its curses.

etymology_text: Derived from Latin patria (“fatherland”).

examples.text: Ma, kuando se akodro ke el valiante Amadis no kedo satisfecho de yamarse solo “Amadis” i adjusto el nombre de su reynado i patria para darle fama, i se yamo “Amadis de Gaula”, I el kijo azer lo mizmo, komo un buen kavayero, adjustar al suyo el nombre de la suya, i yamarse “don Kishot de la Mancha”, ke asegun el, deklarava klaramente su linaje i patria, i la onorava en tomandola por alkunya.
examples.ref: 2013, Myriam Moscona, Jacobo Sefamí with Martín Fierro, José Hernández, Por mi boka: Textos de la diáspora sefardí en ladino, Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial México, →ISBN, page 222:
examples.english: Nevertheless, when [someone] remembered that the valiant Amadis was left unsatisfied in merely being called ‘Amadis’, [he] added the name of his kingdom and homeland to make himself famous, and he called himself ‘Amadis of Gaula’, and he kept repeating himself, like a good knight, adding to his name the name of his homeland, and calling himself ‘don Koshot de la Mancha’, as according to him, it was clearly declaring his lineage and homeland, and he was esteeming it in treating it like family.
examples.translation: Nevertheless, when [someone] remembered that the valiant Amadis was left unsatisfied in merely being called ‘Amadis’, [he] added the name of his kingdom and homeland to make himself famous, and he called himself ‘Amadis of Gaula’, and he kept repeating himself, like a good knight, adding to his name the name of his homeland, and calling himself ‘don Koshot de la Mancha’, as according to him, it was clearly declaring his lineage and homeland, and he was esteeming it in treating it like family.

examples.text: En uno de los dias de Shabat ke estava en su kaza el konto a su mujer ke tuvo "Giluy Eliyau", o sea ke se aparesio en su suenyo Eliyau Anavi, ke le demando de deshar todo i pasar a bivir imediatamente a la sivdad de Tsfat en la Tierra Santa, afin de difundir la Kabala praktika ke el avia dezvelopado, siendo ke le kedavan solamente dos anyos de vida.
examples.ref: 2005, Aki Yerushalayim, volumes 26–28, page 9:
examples.english: One Shabbat as he was in his house, he told his wife that he had "Giluy Eliyau", or maybe it looked like Eliyau Anavi in a dream, ask him to leave everything alone and immediately go live in Tsfat City in the Holy Land in order to propagate the practical Kabbalah that he had developed, seeing as how he had only two years to live.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish diente (“tooth”), from Latin dentem, dēns, from Proto-Italic *dents, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.

examples.text: I arankarvos ojo por ojo, diente por diente.
examples.ref: 2000, Aki Yerushalayim, numbers 62–64, page 95:
examples.english: And settling yourselves eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
examples.translation: And settling yourselves eye for eye, tooth for tooth.

head_templates.expansion: lengua f (Hebrew spelling לינגוה, plural lenguas)

examples.text: “Si me olƀidare de ti, ¡O Yᵉrûšāláyim!, se olƀide mi dereĉa, se apege mi lengua a mi paladar, si no me akordare de ti, si no enaltesiere a Yᵉrûšāláyim soƀre la kaƀesera de mi alegría”
examples.ref: 1979, Isaac ben Michael Badhav, Ana María Riaño López, Un tratado sefardí de moral, Ameller, →ISBN, page 53:
examples.english: If I will forget about you, O Jerusalem, [if] my right is forgotten, [if] my tongue sticks to my palate, if I won’t agree with you, if I do not rise to Jerusalem over the leader of my pleasure.
examples.translation: If I will forget about you, O Jerusalem, [if] my right is forgotten, [if] my tongue sticks to my palate, if I won’t agree with you, if I do not rise to Jerusalem over the leader of my pleasure.

examples.text: Mi primera lengua fue el espanyol muestro, i syempre fue la lengua de famiya.
examples.ref: 2000, La Lettre Sépharade, numbers 1–19, La Lettre Sépharade, page 7:
examples.english: My mother tongue was our Spanish, and it was always our family’s language.
examples.translation: My mother tongue was our Spanish, and it was always our family’s language.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish estomago (“maw”), from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos, “gullet; stomach”), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

examples.text: Kalía solamente kaminando kon metod, por no kansar de ƀista el estómago tan flako, enforteserlo, i para esto era menester un poko de tiempo.
examples.ref: 1978, María del Rosario Martínez González, editor, Un marido entre dos mužeres: novela anónima en ladino, Ameller Ediciones, →ISBN, page 50:
examples.english: One only needed to walk with [this] method: by avoiding rest until the stomach [was] too weak, strengthening it, and a little time was needed for this.
examples.translation: One only needed to walk with [this] method: by avoiding rest until the stomach [was] too weak, strengthening it, and a little time was needed for this.

glosses: stomach (an organ in animals that stores food in the process of digestion)

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish mas (“but”), from Latin magis. Doublet of ma.

examples.text: La madre de mi esfuegra Lea, teniya un ermano muncho mas grande de eya ke se yamava Izak. Izak era el mas grande de los 5 ermanos i era muy seriozo.
examples.ref: 2019 November 27, Eliz Gatenyo, “Las Lentejas Del Onkl Izak”, in Şalom, archived from the original on 29 Oct 2020:
examples.english: My mother-in-law's mother Lea had a brother much bigger than her whose name was Izak. Izak was the biggest of the three brothers and was very serious.

examples.english: The festival of Sukkot that the Pentateuch calls Hag Aasif, the harvest festival, is the most important and the most joyful for an essentially agricultural people as were the people of Israel.

etymology_text:
From Old Spanish lindo, of uncertain origin, but probably from Latin legitimus (“lawful, proper”) through metathesis and assimilation: *lid(i)mo > *limdo > lindo. If so, a doublet of the learned borrowing lejítimo. Corominas considers both lindo and its possible Portuguese cognate lídimo (“legitimate”) as semi-learned terms, but this is uncertain.
Some sources derive it from Latin limpidus (“clean”) instead, but this is less likely for both phonetic and semantic reasons. Old Spanish lindo originally meant “legitimate”, later “authentic, pure, good”, and eventually gave rise to the modern meaning. Moreover, Latin limpidus is already the source of Spanish limpio.

etymology_text: Diminutive of Old Spanish *boño, akin to Spanish buñuelo, Catalan bunyol (both “fritter, doughnut”). The underlying noun is at hand in Catalan bony (“bulge”). Further origin uncertain. Theories include a Gothic *𐌱𐌿𐌲𐌲𐌾𐍉 (*buggjō, “lump”) or identity with Spanish moño (“bun of hair”), itself probably from Paleo-Hispanic.

examples.text: 7 guevos para los gatos, 8 guevos para el Tishpishti, 15 – 20 guevos para la meza de seder, no se kuantos guevos para los bimuelos i mas guevos para las frituras.

examples.english: 7 eggs for the cats, 8 eggs for the Tishpishti, 15-20 eggs for the middle of the Seder, I don't know how many eggs for the bimuelos and more eggs for the fried food.
examples.translation: 7 eggs for the cats, 8 eggs for the Tishpishti, 15-20 eggs for the middle of the Seder, I don't know how many eggs for the bimuelos and more eggs for the fried food.

glosses: A type of fritter eaten by Sephardi Jews during Hanukkah and Pesach.

examples.english: And there were four lepers at the entrance of the gate: and they said one to another: what mean we staying here till we die? etymology_text: From Old Spanish en cuyo mal.

examples.text: “Dizen este byervo kuando avlan de alguna koza triste o de algún muerto i se boltan agora adresándosen a un amigo. Entonses le dizen ‘En kuyo mal’, lo ke kere dezir en espanyol puro: en akel esté el mal. El byervo ‘enkoyamal’ lo dizen tambyén en vezes por burla. Entonses el depende del lashón akódesh ‘im ko yomar’, lo ke iguala a ‘sozum yabaná’” “Enkoyamal...”
examples.ref: 2015 May 14, David M. Bunis, “On Judezmo Terms for the Proverb and Saying”, in library.osu.edu:
examples.english: They say this expression when someone speaks of something sad, such as a death, and then he begins to address his companion. In pure Spanish en cuyo mal means ‘may misfortune be upon him.’ But sometimes ‘enkoyamal’ is said in jest. Then it reflects Hebrew אם כה יאמר [im ko yomar], meaning the same as Turkish sözüm yabana [‘pardon the expression’]” (El Meseret 8, no. 52 [Izmir 1904], p. 5).
examples.translation: They say this expression when someone speaks of something sad, such as a death, and then he begins to address his companion. In pure Spanish en cuyo mal means ‘may misfortune be upon him.’ But sometimes ‘enkoyamal’ is said in jest. Then it reflects Hebrew אם כה יאמר [im ko yomar], meaning the same as Turkish sözüm yabana [‘pardon the expression’]” (El Meseret 8, no. 52 [Izmir 1904], p. 5).

raw_glosses: (Izmir) May misfortune be upon them (expression used in sad occasion or ironically in jest)

examples.text:
Kevrantó, grito amargo y boz de nuestra exclamacion,
Con su intelligencia y su espiritu de abnegacion.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish orgullo (“pride”), borrowed from Old Catalan orgull, from Vulgar Latin *orgollium, itself from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgōllju, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *uzgōljō. Related to French orgueil, Italian orgoglio, & Portuguese orgulho.

examples.text:
Delantre de ti io mi orgolio abato
I mi corason lo razgo con kevranto¹)
examples.ref: 1910, Reuben Eliyahu Israel, Traducsion libera de las poezias ebraicas de Roş Aşana i Kipur, Craiova: Institutul Grafic, I. Samitca şi D. Baraş, Socieatate in Comandita, →OCLC, page 10:
examples.english: I suppress my pride before you, and my heart tears it with despair.
examples.translation: I suppress my pride before you, and my heart tears it with despair.

etymology_text: Most likely a compound of Bulgarian пипер (piper) and чушка (čuška), themselves from Greek πιπέρι (pipéri) and Old Church Slavonic чешоуꙗ (češuja).

examples.text: Los invyernos komiyamos los zerzevates I frutas del invyerno, komo la espinaka, la kol i el apyo. En el enverano era la berendjena, la kalavasa i la pipirushka.
examples.ref: 2006, Los Muestros, numbers 62–69, R. Capuia, page 44:
examples.english: Winters we ate the fruits and vegetables of winter, like spinach, cabbage and celery. In summer it was eggplant, zucchini and green pepper.
examples.translation: Winters we ate the fruits and vegetables of winter, like spinach, cabbage and celery. In summer it was eggplant, zucchini and green pepper.

categories.name: Ladino entries with incorrect language header

examples.text: La seremoniya de inogurasion tendra lugar el lunes 24 de marso venidero.
examples.ref: 2002, Los Muestros, numbers 46–55, R. Capuia, page 6:
examples.english: The inauguration ceremony shall take place the upcoming Monday, March 24.
examples.translation: The inauguration ceremony shall take place the upcoming Monday, March 24.

examples.text: Deskuvrimos defterikos de rabinos kon derushim para shabat o para fiestas relijiozas, defterikos de mo’halim kon poezias kompuestas para algunas okaziones komo inogurasion de kaza mueva o berit mila.
examples.ref: 2005, Aki Yerushalayim, volumes 26–28, page 46:
examples.english: We discover little notebooks from rabbis with sermons for Shabbat or for religious celebrations, little notebooks from uncircumcised ones with poems composed for some occasions such as [a] new house’s inauguration or [a] brit milah.
examples.translation: We discover little notebooks from rabbis with sermons for Shabbat or for religious celebrations, little notebooks from uncircumcised ones with poems composed for some occasions such as [a] new house’s inauguration or [a] brit milah.

categories.name: Ladino entries with incorrect language header

examples.text: […] en el kamino para ir a la inaugurasion de la Şara de Atatürk, kreyemos ke Demirel se sintiria komo en su kaza en bat‐Yam, onde el nombre de Atatürk tiene valor komo en Turkiya.
examples.ref: 1997, Salamon Bicerano, Relatos en lingua judeo-espanyola, Gözlem Gazetecilik Basın ve Yayın A.Ş., →ISBN, page 252:
examples.english: On the way to get to Şara de Atatürk’s inauguration, we believe that Demirel shall be heard as in his house on bat‐Yam, where Atatürk’s name carries weight as in Türkiye.
examples.translation: On the way to get to Şara de Atatürk’s inauguration, we believe that Demirel shall be heard as in his house on bat‐Yam, where Atatürk’s name carries weight as in Türkiye.

examples.text: Mihael Papo eskrivio una gramatika en ebreo i trezlado varias orasiones para la inaugurasion de la Grande Sinagoga sefaradi, en 1808.
examples.ref: 2003, Sefárdica, numbers 14–16, Centro de Investigación y Difusión de la Cultura Sefaradí, page 52:
examples.english: Mihael Papo wrote a grammar in Hebrew and translated various prayers for the Great Sephardi Synagogue’s inauguration in 1808.
examples.translation: Mihael Papo wrote a grammar in Hebrew and translated various prayers for the Great Sephardi Synagogue’s inauguration in 1808.

Por mis reveios²) ke io e reveiado
examples.ref: 1910, Reuben Eliyahu Israel, Traducsion libera de las poezias ebraicas de Roş Aşana i Kipur, Craiova: Institutul Grafic, I. Samitca şi D. Baraş, Socieatate in Comandita, →OCLC, page 10:

examples.translation: I feel agonized and sad through my rebellions that I have resisted.

examples.text: Kuanto a la tersera klase (las povres) no puedemos inkuparla en nada, aunke reprezenta el mas doloriozo espetakulo posivle.
examples.ref: 2006, Miscelánea de estudios árabes y hebraicos, volume 55, Universidad de Granada, page 61:
examples.english: As for the third class (the poor), we cannot fault it for anything, even if it represents the most painful sight possible.
examples.translation: As for the third class (the poor), we cannot fault it for anything, even if it represents the most painful sight possible.

examples.text:

Io dezvii³) mis pasos de tu camino
examples.ref: 1910, Reuben Eliyahu Israel, Traducsion libera de las poezias ebraicas de Roş Aşana i Kipur, Craiova: Institutul Grafic, I. Samitca şi D. Baraş, Socieatate in Comandita, →OCLC, page 10:

examples.text: En konkluzión podemos dizir ke através las enfluensas kulinarias i linguístikas resiprokas entre las varias kuzinas en el tiempo, es posible rekonstruir las fazas de istoria de los puevlos.
examples.ref: 2003, Sefárdica, numbers 14–16, Centro de Investigación y Difusión de la Cultura Sefaradí, page 74:
examples.english: In conclusion, we can say that through the reciprocal linguistic and culinary influences between the various cuisines of the time, it is possible to reconstruct the peoples’ phases of history.
examples.translation: In conclusion, we can say that through the reciprocal linguistic and culinary influences between the various cuisines of the time, it is possible to reconstruct the peoples’ phases of history.

categories.name: Ladino entries with incorrect language header

examples.text: En konkluzion podemos dizir ke los djudios de la Espanya Medievala no se mantenian solamente de ufisios finansiarios i komersales i no todos eran rikos, savios o intelektuales.
examples.ref: 1999, Matilda Koén-Sarano, קורס לספרדית־יהודית (לאדינו) למתקדמים, Merkaz Eliacher, Universidad Ben-Gurion en el Negev, page 156:
examples.english: In conclusion, we can say that Mediaeval Spain’s Jews were not maintained only through financial and commercial offices, and not all were rich, wise, or intellectual.
examples.translation: In conclusion, we can say that Mediaeval Spain’s Jews were not maintained only through financial and commercial offices, and not all were rich, wise, or intellectual.

examples.text: En un sentimiento de respekto por esta admiravle institusion, devemos en konkluzion azer akodrar a nuestros lektores la valor da la edukasion de esta Fondasion ke troko la vida de los judios en los payizes onde fraguo sus eskuolas.
examples.ref: 2000, Salamon Bicerano, Relatos akademikos i populares en Judeo-Espanyol (1998–2000), Gözlem, →ISBN, page 82:
examples.english: In a feeling of respect for this admirable institution, we must, in conclusion, remind our readers this foundation’s education’s value that changes the life of Jews in countries where the foundation built schools.
examples.translation: In a feeling of respect for this admirable institution, we must, in conclusion, remind our readers this foundation’s education’s value that changes the life of Jews in countries where the foundation built schools.

examples.text: Un día yo fui al kabiné (ke era un foyo en al tierra, un poko leshos de muestra kaza), i kual no fue mi orror, kuando lo vidi yeno de unos guzanos blankos enormes.
examples.ref: 2006, Matilda Koén-Sarano, Por el plazer de kontar, page 78:
examples.english: One day I was at the workroom (which was a pit in the earth a little ways from our house), and wasn’t I scared when I saw it full of huge white worms.
examples.translation: One day I was at the workroom (which was a pit in the earth a little ways from our house), and wasn’t I scared when I saw it full of huge white worms.

raw_glosses: (modifying an adjective) a bit; a little; kind of; slightly; somewhat; kinda
glosses: a bit; a little; kind of; slightly; somewhat; kinda

examples.text: Kuando una persona le demandava una bevida, tomava un kopo de la tchintura, lo arrufyava un poko kon la agua de la alkuza i, abokandose eskorria de la redoma por enriva su ombro, un tchorro arresfreskante de limonata.
examples.ref: 1982, Enrique Saporta y Beja, En torno de la torre blanca, Editions Vidas Largas, page 178:
examples.english: When somebody demanded a drink, they took a cup from the belt, sprinkled it with a little water from the container, and — bending over lightly scratching themselves from the bottle above their shoulder — a refreshing burst of lemonade.
examples.translation: When somebody demanded a drink, they took a cup from the belt, sprinkled it with a little water from the container, and — bending over lightly scratching themselves from the bottle above their shoulder — a refreshing burst of lemonade.

examples.text: Aspera un poko, bwen djidyó. Es virgwensa de yirse de noche. Amanyana de manyana, aydes. Aséntese en su lugar.
examples.ref: 1999, David M. Bunis, Moshé Cazés, edited by David M. Bunis, Voices from Jewish Salonika, Misgav Yerushalayim, →ISBN, page 592:
examples.english: Wait a minute, [my] good Jew. It’s a shame to leave at night. The day after tomorrow, go forth. May one settle in one’s place.
examples.translation: Wait a minute, [my] good Jew. It’s a shame to leave at night. The day after tomorrow, go forth. May one settle in one’s place.

examples.text: I alora estos dos, tan mansevos, ja espozos, đenitores, respiravan un poko mas kontentes!
examples.ref: 2018, Laura Papo Bohoreta, edited by María José Cano, Nela Kovačević, La mujer sefardí, Editorial Universidad de Granada, →ISBN, page 86:
examples.english: So these two, being young, now married fathers, breathed a little more easily!
examples.translation: So these two, being young, now married fathers, breathed a little more easily!

raw_glosses: (modifying a verb) some; a bit; a little

examples.text: Kalía solamente kaminando kon metod, por no kansar de ƀista el estómago tan flako, enforteserlo, i para esto era menester un poko de tiempo.
examples.ref: 1978, María del Rosario Martínez González, editor, Un marido entre dos mužeres: novela anónima en ladino, Ameller Ediciones, →ISBN, page 50:
examples.english: One only needed to walk with [this] method: by avoiding rest until the stomach [was] too weak, strengthening it, and a little time was needed for this.
examples.translation: One only needed to walk with [this] method: by avoiding rest until the stomach [was] too weak, strengthening it, and a little time was needed for this.

examples.text: Kale ajustado a esto un poko de agua i un poko de arina…
examples.ref: 2006, Matilda Koén-Sarano, Por el plazer de kontar, page 237:
examples.english: A little water and a little flour needs to be added to this…
examples.translation: A little water and a little flour needs to be added to this…

glosses: a little bit; a little; a bit; some (when followed by de)

examples.text: “Se puede dizir ke la komunidad sefaradi de Viena fue el lider de las otras komunidades sefaradis en el kampo kultural i sientifiko. En Viena se dezvelopo (¹) el sistema edukativo, relijiozo i administrativo de los sefaradis.¹”
examples.ref: 2003, Sefárdica, numbers 14–16, Centro de Investigación y Difusión de la Cultura Sefaradí, page 47:
examples.english: ‘One can say that Vienna’s Sephardic community was the leader of the other Sephardic communities in the cultural and scientific fields. The Sephardim’s educational, religious and administrative system was developed in Vienna.’
examples.translation: ‘One can say that Vienna’s Sephardic community was the leader of the other Sephardic communities in the cultural and scientific fields. The Sephardim’s educational, religious and administrative system was developed in Vienna.’

examples.text: […] se dezveloparon i en siertos kavzos deskayeron i desparesieron las komunidades djudias del kontinente evropeo.

examples.translation: The Jewish communities of the European continent were developed and had in certain cases fallen and vanished.

examples.text: Un djoven, kansado de las muchas orores ke el i su puevlo yevavan de dia en dia a las manos de las bestias umanas, demando kual era la parte ke el Dio tenia en los krimenes i su mankansa de traer djustisia a los kampos i de azer sus deveres para su puevlo: “Tio,” dizia, “porke todas estas orasiones? Porke meldar el kadish para los muertos, el Dio los protejara mas en el paradizo de lo ke izo en la tyerra?”
examples.ref: 1999 May 15, Isaac Jack Lévy, transl., And the World Stood Silent: Sephardic Poetry of the Holocaust, Urbana and Chicago: University of Illinois Press, →ISBN, page 50:
examples.english: A young man, tired of the endless horrors that he and his people endured day in and day out at the hands of human beasts, questioned God’s part in the crimes and His failing to bring justice to the camps and carry out His duties to His people: ‘Uncle,’ he would say. ‘Why all the prayers? Why recite the Kaddish for the dead. Will God protect them more in heaven than He does on earth?’

examples.text: Ma, komo el haham-bashi non kijo ke kada uno lo entienda — porke, al kavo del kavo, situasion fue bien delikada siendo ke el dezdichado agora, komo uno d'eyos, podia kontar a la proteksion de las autoridades turkas - alugar de ekrivirles el pesak⁴⁸⁷ en avierto i en largo - el prefiero de kamuflarlo totalmente, eskriviendolo en lashon a-kodesh i en abreviasiones - ansina ke afilu uno ke save bien la letra i la lengva ebrea no lo podia intender paramordi de las abreviasiones, i tambien si deshifrava las abreviasiones non iva a intender muncho mas - porke la fraze ke se resive kvando se deshifren las abreviasiones ez un aviamiento tehniko a kodeks de la ley djudia - i para entenderlo avia ke konoser bien la literatura djudia legal.
examples.ref: 1999, Eliezer Papo, La megila de Saray, E. Papo, page 151:
examples.english: Nonetheless, as the wise chief did not wish for everyone to understand it — since, ultimately, the situation was very delicate, seeing as how the miserable one, like anybody else, could now depend on the Turkish authorities’ protection — instead of writing the psak to them openly and at length — he preferred to completely camouflage it, writing to him in the holy language and in abbreviations — so that even if one understands the letters and the Hebrew tongue well one could not understand it because of the abbreviations, and likewise if one was deciphering the abbreviations one was not going to grasp much else, for the phrase that is received, when the abbreviations are deciphered, is a technicality in the Jewish law’s codex — and to understand it one had to be very familiar with Jewish legal literature.
examples.translation: Nonetheless, as the wise chief did not wish for everyone to understand it — since, ultimately, the situation was very delicate, seeing as how the miserable one, like anybody else, could now depend on the Turkish authorities’ protection — instead of writing the psak to them openly and at length — he preferred to completely camouflage it, writing to him in the holy language and in abbreviations — so that even if one understands the letters and the Hebrew tongue well one could not understand it because of the abbreviations, and likewise if one was deciphering the abbreviations one was not going to grasp much else, for the phrase that is received, when the abbreviations are deciphered, is a technicality in the Jewish law’s codex — and to understand it one had to be very familiar with Jewish legal literature.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish suenno, from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos. Compare Portuguese sono, Italian sonno (“sleep”) and Sicilian sonnu (“sleep”).

examples.text: No me vino el suenyo i no pudi durmir pensando al refran : " Entrada apegada" : a penas empesimos a komer, telefono mi nyeta yamando su padre ke baya a su kaza azer un trabaho.
examples.ref: 1994, Los Muestros, number 16, R. Capuia, page 58:
examples.english: Sleep did not come to me and, thinking of the saying ‘Attached entry’, I could not sleep. We barely started eating, I telephoned my granddaughter calling for her dad so that he may go home to work.
examples.translation: Sleep did not come to me and, thinking of the saying ‘Attached entry’, I could not sleep. We barely started eating, I telephoned my granddaughter calling for her dad so that he may go home to work.

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish suenno, from Latin somnium (“dream”), a derivative of somnus (“sleep”) (as Etymology 1). Compare Portuguese sonho, Italian sogno (“dream”) and Sicilian sonnu (“dream”).

examples.text: Una noche tuvo un suenyo estranyo.
examples.ref: 2002, Aki Yerushalayim, numbers 68–72, page 62:
examples.english: One night he had a strange dream.
examples.translation: One night he had a strange dream.

examples.text: En uno de los dias de Shabat ke estava en su kaza el konto a su mujer ke tuvo "Giluy Eliyau", o sea ke se aparesio en su suenyo Eliyau Anavi, ke le demando de deshar todo i pasar a bivir imediatamente a la sivdad de Tsfat en la Tierra Santa, afin de difundir la Kabala praktika ke el avia dezvelopado, siendo ke le kedavan solamente dos anyos de vida.
examples.ref: 2005, Aki Yerushalayim, volumes 26–28, page 9:
examples.english: One Shabbat as he was in his house, he told his wife that he had "Giluy Eliyau", or maybe it looked like Eliyau Anavi in a dream, ask him to leave everything alone and immediately go live in Tsfat City in the Holy Land in order to propagate the practical Kabbalah that he had developed, seeing as how he had only two years to live.
examples.translation: One Shabbat as he was in his house, he told his wife that he had "Giluy Eliyau", or maybe it looked like Eliyau Anavi in a dream, ask him to leave everything alone and immediately go live in Tsfat City in the Holy Land in order to propagate the practical Kabbalah that he had developed, seeing as how he had only two years to live.

glosses: dream (imaginary events seen in the mind while sleeping)

etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish bello, in turn a borrowing from Old Occitan bel, bell, from Latin bellus. According to Coromines and Pascual, first attested in the early 13th century, but neither in the Poem of the Cid nor in preliterary Castilian. Part of the evidence for it being a borrowing is the lack of diphthongization, cf. Old Spanish castiello, amariello. The native Old Spanish terms were bellido and fermoso.
